title: OSHA vs MSHA: how do their training requirements differ?
description: OSHA spreads training duties across hazard specific standards; MSHA requires every miner to complete set hours of new miner, refresher and task training.
shortAnswer: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) has no single training rule: duties sit inside individual standards, each with its own trigger, content and records. The Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) regulates mines and requires every miner to be trained under a written plan with fixed minimum hours: 24 or 40 hours of new miner training depending on the mine and the rule, at least 8 hours of annual refresher training, and task training before new tasks.
keyTakeaways: The two agencies do not overlap by design: section 4(b)(1) of the OSH Act excludes working conditions that another federal agency regulates, and MSHA regulates mines under the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977.
OSHA training duties are hazard based and scattered across standards in Title 29 of the Code of Federal Regulations; MSHA training duties are person based and consolidated in 30 CFR Parts 46 and 48.

MSHA fixes hours: at least 24 hours of new miner training under Part 46, 40 hours for new underground miners and 24 for new surface miners under Part 48, and at least 8 hours of annual refresher training.
OSHA refresher cycles vary by standard, from annual (bloodborne pathogens) to at least every three years (forklift operator evaluation) to change triggered only.
A 1979 interagency agreement sets out how the two agencies divide authority at and around mine sites and how disputes are resolved.

sections.heading: What is the core difference between OSHA and MSHA training requirements?

blocks.text: The core difference is structure. OSHA attaches training to hazards: if a standard applies to a task, its training rules apply to the workers doing it. MSHA attaches training to people: every miner must complete defined categories of training, with minimum hours, under the operator's written training plan.

Under [section 5 of the OSH Act](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/oshact/section5-duties), employers must keep the workplace free from recognized serious hazards and comply with OSHA standards. OSHA's publication [Training Requirements in OSHA Standards](https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/osha2254.pdf) collects the training provisions found across those standards and states that required training must be provided by and paid for by employers. The general picture is on [OSHA training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements).

MSHA, part of the US Department of Labor, [carries out](https://www.msha.gov/about/mission) the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977 (Mine Act), as amended by the MINER Act of 2006. Its training rules are in [30 CFR Part 46](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-30/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-46), for shell dredging, sand, gravel, surface stone, surface clay, colloidal phosphate and surface limestone mines, and [30 CFR Part 48](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-30/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-48), for other mines, with separate subparts for underground and surface miners. See [MSHA miner training requirements](/regulations/msha-miner-training-requirements).

sections.heading: How do OSHA and MSHA divide jurisdiction?

blocks.text: MSHA regulates working conditions at mines, and OSHA steps back where MSHA has authority. The boundary comes from the OSH Act itself and from a written agreement between the two agencies.

Section 4(b)(1) of the OSH Act provides that ['nothing in this Act shall apply to working conditions of employees with respect to which other Federal agencies'](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/oshact/section_4) exercise statutory authority to prescribe or enforce occupational safety or health standards. Because the Mine Act gives MSHA that authority over mines, OSHA standards generally do not apply to mine working conditions that MSHA covers.

The [1979 Interagency Agreement between MSHA and OSHA](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/mou/1979-03-29) delineates areas of authority, sets factors for deciding coverage on grounds of convenience of administration and provides a procedure for jurisdictional questions. It states that OSHA applies where the Mine Act provisions do not cover or otherwise do not apply. Disputes go first to the MSHA District Manager and the OSHA Regional Administrator or State designee, then to national offices and, if needed, to the Secretary of Labor.

blocks.title: Practical consequence
blocks.text: For operations near the boundary, such as processing facilities, contractors moving between mine and non mine sites, or maintenance shops, confirm in writing which agency covers each location before building the training matrix. The training models are different enough that the wrong assumption produces the wrong curriculum.
If the work is at a mine within MSHA's authority, MSHA training rules apply; otherwise OSHA or a State Plan applies. Many groups run both regimes at once across different sites.

items: **Sand, gravel and surface aggregate operations:** Part 46. Build the written training plan, 24 hour new miner training with the timing rules in section 46.5, 8 hour annual refresher and task training.
**Underground mines and other surface mines:** Part 48, with 40 hour pre work training for new underground miners and 24 hours for new surface miners.
**Non mine sites in the same group:** OSHA or the relevant State Plan, mapped standard by standard. Corporate offices, warehouses and plants away from the mine fall here.

**International groups:** Australian mines follow state mining safety laws alongside work health and safety laws; see [OSHA vs WHS](/compare/osha-vs-whs) for the general comparison and [how to build a training matrix for a mining operation](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix-for-a-mining-operation).

sections.heading: How can one training matrix cover both regimes?

blocks.text: Organize by worker and site: every person at an MSHA site gets the MSHA categories, and every hazard at an OSHA site gets its standard's rules. The illustrative mapping below shows a group running a quarry and a downstream plant.

blocks.text: A [training matrix](/glossary/training-matrix) that links roles, sites and rules keeps the two regimes apart without duplicating content. For safety critical tasks, add [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency) so records show capability as well as hours.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each site, role and task to the MSHA or OSHA provisions that govern it, with provenance to the regulation text, before content is written. Shared hazard knowledge is defined once and reused, while each regime's hours, triggers and record formats stay attached to the obligation they come from.

faqs.q: Do OSHA Outreach 10 and 30 hour cards count toward MSHA training?
faqs.a: No. OSHA states that its Outreach Training Program is voluntary, does not meet the training requirements of any OSHA standard and is not a certification. MSHA training must follow the operator's written plan under Part 46 or Part 48, with the required subjects and hours.

faqs.q: How long must MSHA training records be kept?
faqs.a: Under section 46.9, annual refresher records must be kept for two years and all training records for at least 60 days after a miner's employment ends. Under Part 48, certificates for current miners are kept at the mine site for two years or 60 days after termination. Records use Form 5000-23 or an equivalent with a false certification warning.

faqs.q: Does MSHA require training to be paid?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 46.10 requires training to be provided during normal working hours and miners to be paid at their normal rate while taking it. OSHA's guidance similarly states that training required by OSHA standards must be provided by and paid for by employers.

For penalties assessed after January 15, 2026, OSHA lists maximums of $16,550 per serious or other than serious violation, $16,550 per day for failure to abate, and $165,514 per willful or repeated violation. The figures are adjusted for inflation each year.
